Part 1 of 6

Why England Wanted Colonies

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Identify the economic, political, and religious motivations of English monarchs and investors for the establishment of American colonies.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, what three kinds of reasons pushed England to start colonies?

Reading APrivate Business Ventures

The English colonies were thus private business ventures or religious experiments—or, in some instances, both. Because few people were wealthy enough to finance a colony, those interested in colonization banded together to share the financial risks. Under this strategy, investors purchased shares of stock in a colony to form joint-stock companies. They raised large amounts of money and protected individual investors from complete loss if a colony failed. If a colony succeeded, investors would share the profits.

Although the English colonies were independent ventures, the English government wanted them to provide raw materials such as timber for shipbuilding, tobacco for smoking, and fur pelts for hats and coats. It also wanted the colonists to buy English-made goods such as textiles, furniture, tea, and other luxuries.

Word help: finance = pay for · shares of stock = small pieces of a company that people buy · investors = people who put in money to make more money · raw materials = natural goods like wood, tobacco, and furs

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “The English Background” (People and Profits) (p. 56).

Reading BA Safety Valve and the Promise of Land

Moreover, the English monarchs viewed the colonies as a safety valve to relieve social pressures at home. For decades, peasants had been pushed off the land by the enclosure movement, in which landlords found it more profitable to raise sheep than to host poor farmworkers and so had evicted many peasants. . . . The most powerful enticements for prospective colonists were the possibility of acquiring land and the promise of a better life: what later came to be called “the American dream.” Land was America’s prized treasure—once it was taken from the Indigenous populations.

Word help: monarchs = kings and queens · safety valve = a way to let out pressure · peasants = poor farmworkers · evicted = forced out of their homes · enticements = things that attract people

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “The English Background” (People and Profits).

Reading CThe Puritans Leave England

The Puritans wanted to simplify religion to its most basic elements: people worshipping God in plain, self-governing congregations without the formal trappings of Catholic and Anglican ceremonies. They had hoped the new king would support their efforts. However, James I, who had been baptized in the Catholic faith, embraced the conservative Anglican Church and sought to imprison or banish the Puritans. . . . Many Puritans left England, and some, who would later be known as Pilgrims (people who travel to foreign lands), sailed to America.

Word help: congregations = church groups · Anglican = the official Church of England · banish = force someone to leave the country

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “The English Background” (Religious Conflict and War).

Picture 1A 1609 Advertisement for Virginia

The Virginia Company printed this pamphlet in London in 1609 to get people to move to Virginia. The words say: “Offering most excellent fruits by planting in Virginia. Exciting all such as be well affected to further the same.” (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: Nova Britannia = “New Britain” · excellent fruits = great rewards · planting = starting farms and settlements · the ship = the way people would get to Virginia

Norton, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies,” caption: “Virginia Company. This pamphlet was printed in London in 1609 to promote immigration to Virginia.” Primary source.

Part 2 of 6

The Chesapeake and the Carolinas

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Describe the political, economic, social, and religious characteristics of English colonies in the Chesapeake region, New England, the Carolinas, and the middle colonies—Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, and Delaware—before 1700.

IN MY WORDS: In the southern colonies, what crop made money, and who did most of the work?

Reading DJamestown and Tobacco

In December 1606, the Virginia Company sent to America three ships carrying 104 colonists, all men and boys. . . . On a marshy peninsula fed by salty water and swarming with mosquitos, the colonists built a fort, huts, and a church. They struggled to find enough to eat, for some of them were unfamiliar with farming or were “gentleman” adventurers who despised manual labor. Were it not for the food acquired or stolen from neighboring Indigenous groups, Jamestown would have collapsed.

Over the next several years, the Jamestown colony limped along until the settlers found a profitable crop: tobacco. . . . Despite its labor-intensive demands, the growing of tobacco became the most profitable enterprise in colonial Virginia and Maryland. However, large-scale tobacco farming required more land for planting and more laborers to work the fields. Much like sugar and rice, tobacco would become one of the primary crops that ultimately drove the demand for indentured servants and enslaved Africans.

Word help: peninsula = land with water on three sides · despised manual labor = hated working with their hands · collapsed = failed · labor-intensive = needing many workers · indentured servants = workers who worked for years to pay for their trip

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (Jamestown; Tobacco) (p. 61).

Reading ELand, Votes, and Slavery in 1619

In 1618, Sir Edwin Sandys, a prominent member of Parliament, became head of the Virginia Company. His crucial innovation was the launching of a new headright (land grant) policy: anyone who bought a share in the company and could pay for passage to Virginia could have fifty acres upon arrival and fifty more for each servant he brought along.

In 1619, the Virginia Company created the first experiment with representative government in the American colonies. The House of Burgesses, modeled after Parliament, would meet at least once a year to make laws and decide on taxes. . . . The arrival of Africans in Virginia marked the beginning of two and a half centuries of slavery in British North America. . . . The year 1619 thus witnessed the irony of the Virginia colony establishing the principle of representative government while importing enslaved Africans.

Cecilius Calvert envisioned Maryland as a refuge for English Catholics. . . . In the end, Maryland succeeded more quickly than Virginia because of its focus from the start on growing tobacco.

Word help: headright = land given to each person who paid to bring someone to Virginia · passage = the trip by ship · representative government = people elect others to make laws for them · irony = something that seems the opposite of what you expect · refuge = safe place

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (Governance; Slavery in British North America; Maryland).

Reading FThe Carolinas and Barbados

Carolina, the southernmost mainland British American colony in the seventeenth century, began as two widely separated areas that officially became North and South Carolina in 1712. . . . To speed their efforts to generate profits from growing sugarcane, they recruited established English planters from Barbados, the most easterly of the Caribbean “sugar islands,” located about 1,700 miles southeast of Florida. . . . It was widely known for its brutal treatment of enslaved laborers, many of whom were literally worked to death on sugar plantations.

In fact, so many of the enslaved laborers in Barbados died from overwork, poor nutrition, and disease that the sugar planters capitalized on the transatlantic slave trade to regularly replace them with newly imported enslaved people. . . . Many seized the chance to settle Carolina and bring with them the Barbadian plantation system.

Rice rather than sugar became the dominant crop in South Carolina because it was perfectly suited to the hot, humid growing conditions. . . . Enslavers used Africans to work their fields not only because the enslaved labor was cheaper but also because of the Africans’ knowledge of rice production and irrigation.

Word help: planters = owners of large farms (plantations) · brutal = very cruel · transatlantic slave trade = buying and shipping enslaved Africans across the Atlantic Ocean · dominant = main · irrigation = bringing water to crops

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (The Carolinas; The Barbados Connection; Profitable Colonies).

Part 3 of 6

New England and the Middle Colonies

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Describe the political, economic, social, and religious characteristics of English colonies in the Chesapeake region, New England, the Carolinas, and the middle colonies—Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, and Delaware—before 1700.

IN MY WORDS: How were New England and the middle colonies different from the southern colonies?

Reading GPuritan New England

Unlike Maryland and Virginia, the “New” England colonies were intended to be self-governing religious utopias.

Since the Mayflower colonists were outside the jurisdiction of any organized government, forty-one of them, all men, resolved to rule themselves. They signed the Mayflower Compact, a covenant (group contract) to form “a civil body politic” based on “just and civil laws” designed “for the general good.” The Mayflower Compact was not democracy in action, however. The saints granted only themselves the rights to vote and hold office.

The Plymouth colony’s population never rose above 7,000, and after ten years it was overshadowed by its much larger neighbor, the Massachusetts Bay Colony. . . . This group sought to create “a City upon a Hill,” as Winthrop declared, borrowing the phrase from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount. . . . Ironically, the same Puritans who had fled persecution in England did not hesitate to persecute people of other religious views in New England.

Word help: utopias = perfect communities · jurisdiction = control of a government · resolved = decided · civil body politic = a government made by the people · saints = here, the church members · persecute = treat people cruelly because of their beliefs

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (New England; Plymouth; Massachusetts Bay).

Reading HThe Salem Witch Trials

In 1692–1693, the growing social and religious strains within the Massachusetts Bay Colony reached a climax in the witchcraft hysteria at Salem Village (now called Danvers). . . . The mass hysteria extended to surrounding towns, and within a few months the Salem Village jail was filled with more than 150 men, women, and children—and two dogs—all accused of practicing witchcraft. . . . By then, nineteen people (fourteen women and five men, including a former minister) had been hanged—all justified by the biblical verse that tells believers not to “suffer a witch to live.”

Word help: strains = stresses · climax = the highest point · hysteria = wild fear that spreads · accused = blamed

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (Witches in Salem).

Reading INew Netherland

Like Virginia and Massachusetts, the New Netherland colony emerged as a profit-making enterprise. “Everyone here is a trader,” explained one resident. And like the French colonists in Canada and along the Mississippi River, the Dutch were mainly interested in the fur trade, as the intense European demand for beaver hats generated huge profits.

Unlike most other European nations with colonies in the Americas, the Dutch embraced ethnic and religious diversity. . . . From its inception, New York City was America’s first multiethnic community—immigrants dominated its population.

Word help: enterprise = business · embraced ethnic and religious diversity = welcomed people of many backgrounds and faiths · inception = beginning

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (The Dutch Republic and Trade).

Reading JPenn’s “Holy Experiment”

Unlike John Winthrop in Massachusetts, Penn encouraged people of different religions from different countries to settle in Pennsylvania. He considered it a “holy experiment” where people of all faiths, nations, and social classes could live together in harmony.

The relations between the Indigenous Americans and the Pennsylvania Quakers were unusually peaceful because of the Quakers’ friendliness and Penn’s policy of purchasing land titles from Indigenous Americans.

In 1702, East and West Jersey were united as the single royal colony of New Jersey. Unlike the Puritan New England colonies, New Jersey promoted religious tolerance, welcoming Catholics, Jews, Lutherans, and Quakers.

Word help: Quakers = a religious group that believed in equality and peace · harmony = peace and agreement · land titles = legal ownership of land · religious tolerance = letting people follow different religions

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (Pennsylvania; New Jersey).

Part 4 of 6

Colonists and Indigenous Peoples

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Analyze the ways in which English colonists and Indigenous Americans responded to each other’s presence.

IN MY WORDS: Name two ways colonists and Indigenous peoples dealt with each other (for example: trade, peace, or war).

Reading KThe Powhatan and the “Strangers”

At this time, the Powhatan Confederacy dominated the Indigenous peoples of the Chesapeake region. . . . Wahunsunacock (called “Chief Powhatan”), the chief of the Powhatan, ruled several hundred villages encompassing 6,000 square miles and 14,000 people in eastern Virginia.

In fact, Wahunsunacock was as much a dominant ruler as the English or Spanish monarchs. . . . Upon learning of the English settlement at Jamestown, he planned to impose his will on the “Strangers” as well. . . . Only too late would Wahunsunacock realize that the English had come to Virginia not to trade with but rather “to invade my people and possess my country.”

By 1616, the discovery that tobacco flourished in Virginia intensified the settlers’ lust for even more land. . . . In 1622, the Indigenous Americans tried to repel the land-grabbing English. . . . The English retaliated by decimating the Indigenous American populations of Virginia.

Word help: confederacy = a group of nations joined together · encompassing = covering · impose his will = force others to obey · repel = push back · retaliated = struck back · decimating = killing large numbers of

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Settling the American Colonies” (The Powhatan Confederacy). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Indigenous Peoples and English Settlers” (Food and Land).

Reading LBacon’s Rebellion (1676)

In the mid-1670s, simmering tensions caused by falling tobacco prices (stemming from overproduction), rising taxes, and crowds of landless freed servants sparked what came to be called Bacon’s Rebellion. . . . In 1676, when Governor William Berkeley refused to attack the raiders, Bacon organized a rebel group to terrorize the “protected and darling Indians.” He pledged to kill all the Indigenous people in Virginia and promised to free any servants and enslaved individuals who joined him.

The rebellion became a battle of landless servants, small farmers, and even enslaved Africans against Virginia’s wealthiest planters and political leaders.

Bacon, however, fell ill from dysentery and died a month later, after which the rebellion disintegrated.

Word help: simmering = slowly building · landless = owning no land · pledged = promised · dysentery = a deadly stomach disease · disintegrated = fell apart

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Indigenous Peoples and English Settlers” (Bacon’s Rebellion).

Source FThe King Answers Bacon’s Rebellion (Primary Source)

King Charles II issued this proclamation on October 27, 1676, after Bacon’s Rebellion. It offered a reward, a pardon, and freedom. The spelling is from 1676.

“His Majesty doth hereby Declare, That such Person or Persons as shall Apprehend the said Nathaniel Bacon, and him shall bring before His Majesties Governor . . . shall have as a Reward from His Majesties Royal Bounty, the sum of Three Hundred Pounds Sterling. . . . That then such of the Servants or Slaves of such persons so persisting and continuing such Rebellion, as shall render themselves to, and take up Arms under His Majesties Governor . . . shall have their Liberty, and be for ever Discharged and Free from the Service of the said Offenders.”

Word help: His Majesty = the king · doth = does · apprehend = capture · Pounds Sterling = English money · persisting = keeping on · render themselves = turn themselves in · take up Arms = fight · Liberty = freedom · Offenders = the rebels

“By the King, A Proclamation for the suppression of a rebellion lately raised within the Plantation of Virginia,” October 27, 1676. In Norton, Ch. 2, “Indigenous Peoples and English Settlers,” Comparing Perspectives: “Bacon’s Rebellion and the Intersection of Gender, Race, and Class.”

Source F. (1) What reward did the king offer for capturing Bacon? (2) What did he offer to servants and enslaved people of rebels who turned themselves in and fought for the governor?

Point of view. Bacon promised freedom to servants and enslaved people who joined him. The king promised freedom to those who left the rebels. Why would both sides make the same kind of promise?

Reading MWar in New England

In 1636, settlers in Massachusetts accused a Pequot man of murdering a colonist; they took revenge by setting fire to a Pequot village. . . . As the residents fled the flames, the Puritans killed them—men, women, and children.

Indigenous American leaders—especially the chief of the Wampanoag Nation, Metacom (known to the colonists as King Philip)—as well as Nipmuc, Pocumtuck, and Narragansett people resented English efforts to take their lands and to convert their people to Christianity. . . . The gruesome violence spun out of control in what came to be called King Philip’s War (1675–1678), or Metacom’s War. The fighting killed more people in proportion to the population than any American conflict since.

The war slashed New England’s Indigenous population in half, dropping it to fewer than 9,000.

Word help: revenge = getting back at someone · resented = were angry about · convert = change someone’s religion · gruesome = horrible · in proportion to = compared with the size of

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Indigenous Peoples and English Settlers” (The Pequot War; King Philip’s War).

Reading NThe Iroquois League

In the interior of New York, however, a different situation arose. There, sometime before 1600, the Iroquois Nations had forged an alliance so strong that the outnumbered Dutch and, later, English traders were forced to work with them to acquire beaver pelts. . . . During the first half of the eighteenth century, they stayed out of the almost constant wars between the English and French, which enabled them to play the two European powers against each other while creating a thriving fur trade for themselves.

Word help: interior = inland, away from the coast · forged an alliance = joined together as partners · outnumbered = had fewer people · play ... against each other = use two rivals to get what you want

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Indigenous Peoples and English Settlers” (The Iroquois League).

Part 5 of 6

The Strongest Colonies by 1700

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Explain how the English colonies became the most populous, prosperous, and powerful region in North America by 1700.

IN MY WORDS: Give one reason the English colonies grew bigger and stronger than the French and Spanish colonies.

Reading OThriving Colonies

By the early eighteenth century, England’s colonies had outstripped those of both the French and the Spanish as tensions among the three major European powers grew. English America, both the mainland colonies and those in the Caribbean, had become the most populous, prosperous, and powerful of the European empires’ colonial holdings. Although some settlers found hard labor, desperation, and an early death in America, others flourished only because they were able to exploit Indigenous people, indentured servants, or Africans.

The English colonists enjoyed crucial advantages over their European rivals. The tightly controlled colonial empires created by the monarchs of Spain and France stifled innovation. By contrast, the English and Dutch organized colonies as profit-making enterprises with a minimum of royal control. . . . Perhaps most important, the English colonies enjoyed a greater degree of self-government, which made them more dynamic and innovative than their French and Spanish counterparts.

Word help: outstripped = got ahead of · populous = having many people · prosperous = rich · flourished = did very well · exploit = use unfairly for your own gain · stifled innovation = stopped new ideas · self-government = people running their own affairs

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 2, “Thriving Colonies” (p. 97).
